long_definition: An older methodology (1990s) that influenced later agile thinking; still occasionally referenced when contrasting fast, iterative approaches with heavier, plan-driven ones.

short_definition: A demonstration of newly completed work shown to stakeholders, typically at the end of a sprint or release cycle.
long_definition: See Sprint Review — often used interchangeably; the point is showing working software to get feedback and validate direction, not just reporting status.

short_definition: A regular team meeting (typically at the end of a sprint) to reflect on what went well, what didn't, and what to improve.
long_definition: One of the core Scrum ceremonies; distinct from a Sprint Review — the retro is about the team's process, not the product output.

short_definition: Commonly known as SAFe — a framework for applying Agile and Lean practices across large organizations with many teams working on interdependent products.
long_definition: Provides structure for coordinating multiple Scrum teams (via constructs like the Agile Release Train) at enterprise scale; more prescriptive and process-heavy than team-level Scrum, which is both its main appeal and its main criticism.

short_definition: The gradual, often unapproved expansion of a project's requirements beyond what was originally agreed.
long_definition: A common cause of missed deadlines; managed by having a clear scope baseline and a deliberate process for evaluating and approving any additions.

short_definition: An Agile framework organizing work into fixed-length sprints, with defined roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team) and ceremonies (planning, daily standup, review, retrospective).
long_definition: The most widely adopted specific implementation of Agile values; provides more structure and prescribed process than the broader Agile philosophy alone.

short_definition: Any of the standard Scrum ceremonies (daily standup, sprint planning, review, retrospective).
long_definition: Used loosely to refer to Scrum's regular meeting cadence; most often specifically means the Daily Scrum/standup.

short_definition: A hybrid approach combining Scrum's structure (roles, ceremonies) with Kanban's continuous-flow, WIP-limited board.
long_definition: Popular with teams that want some Scrum discipline (like regular retrospectives) without committing to strict, fixed-length sprints.

short_definition: Basecamp's product development methodology using fixed six-week cycles, 'appetite'-based scoping (time budget first, not detailed spec), and no backlog grooming.
long_definition: A notable departure from Scrum — instead of estimating how long a well-defined feature takes, teams decide how much time they're willing to spend and shape the solution to fit.

short_definition: A fixed, time-boxed period (commonly two weeks) during which a Scrum team commits to completing a set amount of work.
long_definition: The core rhythm of Scrum — provides a predictable cadence for planning, delivering, and reviewing work, and a regular checkpoint for adjusting priorities.

short_definition: The set of items a team has committed to completing during the current sprint, pulled from the broader product backlog.
long_definition: Distinct from the product backlog (the full list of everything that might get built eventually) — the sprint backlog is the specific, committed slice for this cycle.

short_definition: A short statement describing the overarching objective a team is trying to achieve in a given sprint.
long_definition: Gives a sprint's individual stories a shared purpose, and provides a basis for the team to make tradeoff calls if not everything planned can be completed.

short_definition: A ceremony at the start of a sprint where the team decides what work to commit to and how they'll approach it.
long_definition: Sets the Sprint Backlog and, ideally, a clear Sprint Goal — the foundational planning event for the cycle ahead.

short_definition: The amount of work (usually measured in story points) a team completes per sprint, tracked over time.
long_definition: See Velocity — used to forecast how much work a team can realistically commit to in future sprints, based on historical throughput.

short_definition: Short form for Daily Scrum/Daily Standup — a brief daily team sync.
long_definition: See Daily Scrum.

short_definition: A single unit of relative sizing used to estimate the effort/complexity of a user story.
long_definition: See Story Points.

short_definition: An abstract, relative unit teams use to estimate the size or complexity of a user story, rather than estimating hours directly.
long_definition: Deliberately relative (a 5 is roughly twice a 2-3) rather than absolute, which tends to produce more consistent estimates than trying to predict exact hours, especially for creative/uncertain work.

short_definition: A simplified relative-estimation technique using size categories (XS, S, M, L, XL) instead of numeric story points.
long_definition: Faster and lower-precision than Fibonacci-based story pointing — useful for high-level roadmap estimation where exact numbers aren't needed yet.

short_definition: A short, plain-language description of a feature from the end user's perspective, typically in the format 'As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit].'
long_definition: Keeps requirements focused on user value rather than technical implementation; paired with Acceptance Criteria to define when the story is complete.

short_definition: A team's average rate of completing work (typically measured in story points) per sprint.
long_definition: Used for forecasting and sprint planning, but a poor metric for comparing teams against each other since point scales aren't standardized across teams.

short_definition: A traditional, linear software development approach where each phase (requirements, design, build, test, release) is completed fully before the next begins.
long_definition: Contrasted with Agile's iterative approach; still used for projects with well-understood, stable requirements and heavy dependency/compliance needs, but criticized for making it costly to change direction once a phase is done.

short_definition: The formal name for the Waterfall development approach.
long_definition: See Waterfall.

short_definition: A prioritization method (used in SAFe) that scores work by dividing Cost of Delay by job size, prioritizing items with the best 'value per unit of effort, adjusted for urgency.'
long_definition: A more economically rigorous approach than simple stack-ranking — explicitly weighs urgency (cost of delay) against effort rather than treating all backlog items as equally time-sensitive.

short_definition: A growth framework tracking five stages of the customer lifecycle: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
long_definition: Coined by Dave McClure ('Pirate Metrics' from the AARRR acronym). Gives growth-focused teams a shared vocabulary and structure for diagnosing where in the funnel they're losing users.

short_definition: The stage of the customer lifecycle where a new user first discovers and signs up for a product.
long_definition: The first stage of the AARRR framework — measured by channels and cost (see Customer Acquisition Cost) that bring in new users.

short_definition: The point at which a new user experiences the product's core value for the first time — the 'aha moment.'
long_definition: The second stage of AARRR; often the highest-leverage stage to optimize, since a user who never activates was never really acquired in a meaningful sense.

short_definition: See Product Analytics — the practice of measuring and analyzing user behavior within a product.
long_definition: See Product Analytics.

short_definition: The average annualized value of a customer contract, commonly used in B2B/enterprise sales to normalize deals of different lengths.
long_definition: Distinct from ARR (which is the aggregate across all customers) — ACV describes a single deal's annualized worth, often used to segment and prioritize sales/account efforts.

short_definition: Average Revenue Per User — total revenue divided by the number of active users or accounts over a given period.
long_definition: A standard SaaS/subscription metric for understanding monetization efficiency; often segmented by user cohort or plan tier to spot where revenue is concentrated.

short_definition: The value of recurring revenue a subscription business expects to receive over a 12-month period.
long_definition: A core SaaS health metric, used to track growth and communicate scale to investors; distinct from total revenue since it excludes one-time fees.

short_definition: The technology, processes, and practices used to collect, analyze, and present business data to support decision-making.
long_definition: PMs interact with BI through dashboards and reporting tools built on top of product and business data — understanding what's in the BI stack helps a PM ask for the right metrics.

short_definition: The rate at which customers stop using or paying for a product over a given period.
long_definition: One of the most closely watched metrics in subscription businesses — high churn undermines growth even with strong acquisition, since the business is a leaky bucket.

short_definition: The percentage of customers (or revenue) lost over a specific period, typically monthly or annually.
long_definition: See Churn — 'churn rate' is the formal metric version, usually calculated as customers lost divided by customers at the start of the period.

short_definition: Groups of users who share a common characteristic or starting point in time (e.g., 'users who signed up in January'), analyzed together.
long_definition: Cohort analysis lets teams see how behavior (like retention) changes over time for a defined group, which is more informative than aggregate metrics that can mask trends.

short_definition: The percentage of users who complete a desired action (like signing up or purchasing) out of all who had the opportunity to.
long_definition: A fundamental funnel metric used to evaluate and A/B test changes at any step of a user's journey, from ad click to checkout.

short_definition: The average cost of acquiring one new customer, including marketing and sales spend.
long_definition: Typically evaluated alongside Lifetime Value (LTV) — a healthy business generally needs LTV to significantly exceed CAC (commonly cited as a 3:1 ratio or better) for the growth model to be sustainable.

short_definition: The overall perception a customer has of a company based on all their interactions across the full relationship, not just the product.
long_definition: Broader than UX — includes support, billing, sales, and every other touchpoint. PMs influence CX through the product but don't fully own it.

short_definition: The total revenue a business expects to earn from a customer over the entire relationship.
long_definition: See Lifetime Value (LTV) — same concept, alternate abbreviation.

short_definition: A metric measuring how satisfied customers are with a product, service, or specific interaction, typically via a short post-interaction survey.
long_definition: Simpler and more transactional than NPS — usually asked right after a specific experience (like a support ticket) rather than about overall loyalty.

short_definition: A discipline (and often a dedicated team) focused on proactively helping customers achieve their desired outcomes with a product, to drive retention and expansion.
long_definition: Common in B2B SaaS; overlaps with product in caring about adoption and retention, but Customer Success typically owns the direct relationship and intervention, while product owns the underlying experience.

short_definition: The practice of examining data to draw conclusions and inform decisions.
long_definition: In product work, this spans everything from simple dashboard review to more advanced statistical or predictive analysis of user behavior.

short_definition: Making decisions primarily based on data analysis rather than intuition or opinion.
long_definition: A widely championed but often overstated ideal — most strong product decisions blend data with judgment and qualitative research, since data alone rarely tells you why something is happening or what to do about it.

short_definition: The number of unique users who engage with a product on a given day.
long_definition: A core engagement metric, often tracked alongside MAU (Monthly Active Users); the DAU/MAU ratio is a common proxy for how 'sticky' or habit-forming a product is.

short_definition: A measure of how actively users interact with a product, often expressed as a percentage of users taking a defined action.
long_definition: Definition varies a lot by product and context (opens, time spent, actions taken) — important to be specific about what's being measured rather than treating 'engagement' as one universal number.

short_definition: A visualization of the sequential steps users take toward a goal (like signup or purchase), showing where drop-off occurs at each stage.
long_definition: A foundational tool for diagnosing conversion problems — narrowing at any step highlights exactly where to focus optimization effort.

short_definition: Applying game-like elements (points, badges, leaderboards, progress bars) to a non-game product to boost engagement or motivation.
long_definition: Effective when it reinforces genuinely valuable behavior; criticized when used superficially to manipulate engagement metrics without real user benefit.

short_definition: A mindset and set of fast, often unconventional, low-cost tactics aimed at rapid user or revenue growth, typically blending marketing, product, and data skills.
long_definition: Associated with early-stage startups needing to find scalable growth channels quickly; can blur into product work when the 'hack' is a product feature (like a referral mechanic) rather than a marketing campaign.

short_definition: Self-reinforcing cycles where an output of the product (e.g., invited users) becomes an input that drives more growth, without needing new marketing spend each cycle.
long_definition: Contrasted with a traditional linear funnel — a growth loop compounds because each new user can generate more new users (e.g., viral referral mechanics, user-generated content driving SEO).

short_definition: A single instance of content (like an ad or a piece of content) being displayed to a user.
long_definition: A basic unit of measurement in advertising/marketing analytics — distinct from a click or conversion, which requires the user to actually act.

short_definition: A specific, measurable metric used to evaluate progress toward an important goal.
long_definition: Distinguished from just 'any metric' by being tied directly to a strategic objective and tracked consistently over time — a good KPI set is deliberately small so it stays actionable.

short_definition: The plural of Key Performance Indicator — a set of specific, quantifiable measures used to evaluate progress toward goals.
long_definition: See Key Performance Indicator (KPI).

short_definition: The total revenue a business expects to earn from a single customer over the full duration of their relationship.
long_definition: Central to unit economics — evaluated against Customer Acquisition Cost to determine whether a business's growth model is financially sustainable.

short_definition: The predictable revenue a subscription business expects to receive each month.
long_definition: A core operating metric for SaaS businesses, tracked closely for growth trends; ARR is simply MRR multiplied by 12 for an annualized view.

short_definition: A metric measuring customer loyalty, based on how likely customers are to recommend a product to others (scored 0-10, with promoters, passives, and detractors).
long_definition: Widely used but also widely criticized as an oversimplified single number; still valuable as a longitudinal trend indicator and conversation-starter for qualitative follow-up.

short_definition: The single metric a team or company uses as the primary measure of the value it's delivering, that all other metrics ladder up to.
long_definition: The idea (popularized in growth circles) is that a well-chosen North Star metric aligns cross-functional teams around a shared definition of success, rather than every team optimizing a different local metric.

short_definition: A goal-setting framework pairing a qualitative Objective (what you want to achieve) with measurable Key Results (how you'll know you got there).
long_definition: Popularized by Intel and later Google; designed to align teams around ambitious, measurable goals with regular check-ins, distinct from KPIs, which track ongoing health rather than time-bound stretch goals.

short_definition: Tailoring a product's content, features, or experience to an individual user's characteristics, behavior, or preferences.
long_definition: Ranges from simple (showing a user's name) to sophisticated (algorithmically customized recommendations); a growth and retention lever when done well, but can feel invasive if overdone.

short_definition: Using historical data, statistics, and modeling to forecast future outcomes, like which users are likely to churn.
long_definition: Increasingly built into product analytics tools to flag at-risk users or high-potential opportunities before they materialize, rather than only reporting on what already happened.

short_definition: The extent to which target users start using a product (or a specific feature) and integrate it into their regular workflow.
long_definition: Tracked at both the whole-product level (are people signing up and staying) and the feature level (is this specific feature getting used).

short_definition: The practice and tooling used to track and analyze how users interact with a product.
long_definition: Encompasses event tracking, funnels, cohort analysis, and dashboards — the data infrastructure PMs rely on to make data-informed decisions.

short_definition: The specific quantitative measures used to track a product's performance and health.
long_definition: Umbrella term covering everything from engagement and retention to conversion and revenue metrics, tailored to what matters for a given product.

short_definition: Descriptive, non-numeric data capturing the 'why' behind user behavior — feedback, opinions, observed context.
long_definition: Complements Quantitative metrics; qualitative data explains the reasons behind the numbers a quantitative dashboard shows.

short_definition: Numeric, measurable data such as counts, rates, and percentages used to track product performance.
long_definition: The 'what' side of product measurement — needs pairing with qualitative data to fully understand the reasons behind the numbers.

short_definition: The stage of the customer lifecycle where existing users recommend the product to others, driving new acquisition.
long_definition: The fourth stage of AARRR; a strong referral loop can significantly lower a company's effective Customer Acquisition Cost.

short_definition: The degree to which a product keeps users coming back and continuing to use it over time.
long_definition: Often considered the single most important health signal for a product, since it's a leading indicator of whether the product is actually delivering ongoing value.

short_definition: The percentage of users who continue using a product over a given period, typically measured against a starting cohort.
long_definition: The formal metric version of Retention — commonly visualized as a retention curve showing how usage decays (or stabilizes) over time after signup.

short_definition: Resources (time, money, effort) already invested that cannot be recovered, regardless of future decisions.
long_definition: Referenced in product strategy discussions as a bias to avoid: past investment shouldn't be a reason to continue a failing initiative — the 'sunk cost fallacy' is a common decision-making trap.

short_definition: The rate at which employees leave an organization over a given period (or, in some usage, the rate customers leave — overlapping with churn).
long_definition: In a PM/HR context it usually refers to staff turnover; worth clarifying which meaning is intended given the term's overlap with Churn Rate in some sources.

short_definition: Content (reviews, posts, videos, etc.) created by a product's users rather than the company itself.
long_definition: A powerful growth lever since it scales content creation without direct cost, and can drive both engagement and organic acquisition through search/social discovery.

short_definition: Metrics that look impressive but don't meaningfully indicate business health or inform decisions — e.g., total signups without context on activation or retention.
long_definition: A caution flag in product measurement: teams are encouraged to prefer actionable metrics tied to real outcomes over numbers that just go up and to the right without explaining why.

short_definition: The degree to which a product's growth is driven by existing users bringing in new users, typically measured by a viral coefficient (how many new users each existing user brings).
long_definition: A viral coefficient above 1 means the user base grows on its own without paid acquisition — rare and highly valuable when genuinely achieved.

short_definition: A simple prioritization tool plotting options on two axes (commonly impact vs. effort) to sort ideas into quadrants like quick wins and time sinks.
long_definition: A fast, visual way to have a prioritization conversation with stakeholders without needing a complex scoring model.

short_definition: A quarterly team health and planning ritual (from Spotify) built around four phases: Discover, Define, Design, and... typically paired with the Spotify 'health check' model for autonomous squads.
long_definition: Associated with Spotify's widely discussed (and widely misapplied) engineering culture model — worth noting many companies that cite 'the Spotify model' never actually operated exactly as often described.

short_definition: A structured questioning technique covering Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How to fully define a problem or requirement.
long_definition: A classic journalism and requirements-gathering technique, useful for making sure a problem statement or spec hasn't skipped an important dimension.

short_definition: A prioritization tool similar to the 2x2 Impact/Effort matrix, sorting initiatives into quadrants (quick wins, major projects, fill-ins, thankless tasks).
long_definition: Functionally very close to the general 2x2 Prioritization Matrix; the specific quadrant labels vary by source.

short_definition: A method for organizing a large number of ideas or data points into groups based on their natural relationships.
long_definition: Commonly used after a brainstorm or research synthesis session to find patterns and themes in a mass of individual sticky notes or feedback items.

short_definition: The act of clustering related ideas or feedback together, the process step that produces an Affinity Diagram.
long_definition: See Affinity Diagram.

short_definition: A behavior model (from BJ Fogg's Behavior Design) stating that behavior happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt converge at the same moment.
long_definition: Widely used in product design to diagnose why a desired user action isn't happening — is it a motivation problem, an ability/friction problem, or a missing prompt?

short_definition: A prioritization workshop game where stakeholders are given a limited budget of fake money to 'buy' the features they want most from a priced list.
long_definition: Forces participants to make real tradeoffs rather than just saying yes to everything, since their budget is limited — surfaces genuine priority rather than wish-list requests.

short_definition: A structured framework (from Lewis Lin) for approaching open-ended product design questions: Comprehend, Identify customer, Report needs, Cut through prioritization, List solutions, Evaluate tradeoffs, Summarize.
long_definition: Widely used to prepare for PM interview product design questions, though the underlying structure reflects a reasonable general approach to scoping any product problem.

short_definition: A method for evaluating a decision by comparing its expected costs against its expected benefits.
long_definition: A general business analysis tool used in product prioritization and business case work to compare options on a common footing, though it requires estimating benefits that are often uncertain.

short_definition: A framework clarifying decision-making roles: Driver (leads the process), Approver (makes the final call), Contributors (give input), Informed (kept in the loop).
long_definition: Used to prevent decision paralysis or ambiguity in cross-functional projects by making explicit who actually has authority to decide, versus who just gets consulted.

short_definition: A prioritization tool sorting tasks by urgency and importance into four quadrants, guiding whether to do, schedule, delegate, or drop each one.
long_definition: A general time-management framework (attributed to Dwight Eisenhower) applied in product contexts to separate genuinely important work from merely urgent-feeling noise.

short_definition: A root-cause-analysis technique of asking 'why' repeatedly (typically five times) to drill down from a symptom to its underlying cause.
long_definition: Originated in the Toyota Production System; simple but effective at pushing teams past the first, surface-level explanation of a problem.

short_definition: A lightweight planning framework (Goals, Ideas, Step-projects, Tasks) designed to reduce heavy upfront roadmap planning in favor of faster iteration.
long_definition: Created by Itamar Gilad as an alternative to detailed, long-range roadmaps that tend to become outdated quickly.

short_definition: A framework for defining metrics by first stating a goal, then the questions that need answering to know if it's met, then the specific metrics that answer those questions.
long_definition: Prevents teams from picking metrics first and rationalizing a goal around them — forces metric selection to be driven by what actually needs to be known.

short_definition: A UX measurement framework (from Google) covering Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, and Task success.
long_definition: Gives teams a structured set of categories to choose metrics from when evaluating a product or feature's user experience, rather than defaulting only to business metrics.

short_definition: A four-step framework (from Nir Eyal's 'Hooked') for building habit-forming products: Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, Investment.
long_definition: Used to design features that encourage users to form a repeated usage habit; also cited in critiques of manipulative product design when applied without regard for user benefit.

short_definition: Shorthand reference to Nir Eyal's book and the Hook Model it introduced.
long_definition: See Hook Model.

short_definition: A prioritization framework scoring ideas on Impact, Confidence, and Ease, then multiplying (or averaging) the three to produce a comparable score.
long_definition: Simpler and faster to apply than RICE, at the cost of some precision — a common choice for early-stage or growth teams needing quick relative prioritization.

short_definition: A strategic planning technique that maps a goal to the actors who can affect it, the impacts needed from them, and the deliverables that create those impacts.
long_definition: Created by Gojko Adzic; keeps a roadmap explicitly tied back to a business goal rather than becoming a disconnected list of features.

short_definition: A framework for classifying features into categories — basic expectations, performance features, and delighters — based on how they affect customer satisfaction.
long_definition: Developed by Noriaki Kano; helps prioritization by distinguishing must-haves (whose absence causes dissatisfaction) from delighters (which create disproportionate satisfaction when present but aren't expected).

short_definition: A prioritization technique sorting requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have (this time).
long_definition: Popular for scoping a release or project by forcing explicit agreement on what's truly required versus merely desirable.

short_definition: A method for prioritizing opportunities based on the gap between how important customers say something is and how satisfied they currently are with it.
long_definition: Associated with Outcome-Driven Innovation (Tony Ulwick); high-importance, low-satisfaction areas represent the biggest opportunities for improvement.

short_definition: Plan-Do-Check-Act — a four-step iterative cycle for continuous process improvement.
long_definition: Originated in quality management (associated with W. Edwards Deming); a foundational precursor to many later iterative frameworks, including elements of Agile.

short_definition: The general practice of deciding what to work on first, given limited time and resources.
long_definition: The umbrella activity that all the specific frameworks in this category (RICE, MoSCoW, Kano, etc.) are tools for doing more rigorously and transparently.

short_definition: Prioritization applied specifically to deciding what a product team should build next.
long_definition: See Prioritization — the product-specific application of the broader practice.

short_definition: The category of structured methods (RICE, MoSCoW, Kano, ICE, etc.) used to make product prioritization decisions more systematic.
long_definition: Umbrella term for the specific frameworks catalogued individually elsewhere in this category.

short_definition: A strategic tool mapping how a product's process/technology should evolve relative to its market maturity (adapted from manufacturing's product-process matrix).
long_definition: Less commonly used in software PM than in operations/manufacturing strategy, but occasionally referenced when discussing how process should scale with product maturity.

short_definition: A structured method for translating customer requirements into specific technical/design specifications, often visualized in a 'house of quality' matrix.
long_definition: Originated in manufacturing quality engineering; used in product development to systematically ensure customer needs actually map through to engineering specifications.

short_definition: A prioritization framework scoring initiatives on Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort, combined into a single comparable score.
long_definition: Popularized by Intercom; gives a more granular, quantified alternative to simpler methods like MoSCoW, at the cost of requiring estimates for each factor that can themselves be uncertain.

short_definition: A structured brainstorming technique (from Edward de Bono) where participants deliberately adopt different perspectives — represented by colored 'hats' (facts, emotions, caution, optimism, creativity, process) — to explore a decision.
long_definition: Useful for making sure a group discussion covers multiple angles (risk, opportunity, feelings) rather than getting stuck debating from a single perspective.

short_definition: A goal-setting framework requiring goals to be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
long_definition: A widely used general management tool for making sure goals are concrete enough to actually track and evaluate, rather than vague aspirations.

short_definition: A technique for visually arranging user stories along two dimensions — user journey steps and priority/release — to see the whole product experience at once.
long_definition: Created by Jeff Patton; helps teams avoid a flat, disconnected backlog by keeping stories organized around the actual sequence of user activities.

short_definition: Managing product/engineering organization structure using the 'tribes, squads, chapters, guilds' model associated with Spotify's org design.
long_definition: See 4D Spotify Framework — part of the same widely referenced (and widely adapted or misapplied) organizational model.

short_definition: A prioritization approach plotting initiatives by expected value against implementation complexity to identify the best return-on-effort options.
long_definition: Functionally similar to the Impact/Effort 2x2 Prioritization Matrix, using slightly different axis labels.

short_definition: A prioritization method that scores initiatives across multiple weighted criteria and sums them into a single comparable total.
long_definition: More flexible than fixed frameworks like RICE since teams can define their own criteria and weights, though this also means less standardization across teams or companies.

short_definition: A PM who holds a formal product management certification from a training body (e.g., Pragmatic Institute, Product School, AIPMM).
long_definition: Certification isn't universally required or even highly regarded across the industry, but it can help early-career PMs build foundational knowledge and signal commitment when breaking into the field.

short_definition: The most senior product executive in a company, typically reporting to the CEO and owning overall product strategy and the product organization.
long_definition: Distinguishes a company that treats product as a first-class, board-level function from one where product reports up through engineering or marketing.

short_definition: A team composed of members from different functional disciplines (product, design, engineering, and often data/marketing) working together toward a shared goal.
long_definition: The standard modern product team structure — meant to reduce handoffs and silos by keeping the people who need to collaborate closely in one team rather than separate departments.

short_definition: A PM who specializes in products or platforms centered on data — pipelines, analytics tools, ML infrastructure — often requiring more technical/data fluency than a typical PM role.
long_definition: Common at companies building internal data platforms or data-driven products, where deep familiarity with data infrastructure is core to making good roadmap tradeoffs.

short_definition: A PM focused specifically on digital products (apps, websites, software) as distinct from physical or hybrid products.
long_definition: The term is somewhat redundant in a software-first industry but persists in organizations (e.g., retail, manufacturing) where 'product manager' might otherwise imply a physical product.

short_definition: A PM specializing in fintech products or in internal financial tooling/products, requiring domain expertise in financial systems and regulation.
long_definition: Comes with additional compliance and risk considerations compared to a general PM role, given the regulatory environment around financial products.

short_definition: A designer capable of working across the full range of design disciplines — UX research, interaction design, visual design, and sometimes front-end implementation.
long_definition: Common at smaller companies/teams where a single designer needs to cover ground that would be split across specialists at a larger organization.

short_definition: An engineer capable of working on both the front-end (client-facing UI) and back-end (server, database) layers of an application.
long_definition: PMs benefit from knowing which engineers on their team are full-stack vs. specialized, since it affects how work can be parallelized or who to loop in for a given task.

short_definition: A senior PM role overseeing a group of related products or a team of individual PMs, typically the next level up from a Senior PM.
long_definition: Sits in the product management career ladder between individual-contributor senior PM roles and director-level positions, usually with some people-management responsibility.

short_definition: A specialized product discipline focused specifically on driving growth metrics — acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue — often using rapid experimentation.
long_definition: Distinct from general product management in its explicit focus on growth-loop and funnel metrics as the primary success criteria, rather than broader product experience.

short_definition: A PM specializing in the Growth Product Management discipline.
long_definition: See Growth Product Management — the role title for someone practicing this specialization.

short_definition: A PM specializing in connected/IoT hardware-and-software products, requiring familiarity with both physical device constraints and the software/cloud layer.
long_definition: A hybrid role bridging hardware and software product management, given IoT products typically combine physical devices, connectivity, and a companion app or platform.

short_definition: The discipline of overseeing an organization's information technology systems, infrastructure, and services.
long_definition: Distinct from product management, though PMs building internal tools often work closely with IT management on infrastructure and rollout considerations.

short_definition: A project manager focused specifically on delivering IT initiatives — infrastructure rollouts, system implementations — often with less emphasis on ongoing product strategy than a PM role.
long_definition: More common in traditional enterprise IT organizations than in product-led software companies; focuses on project delivery (scope, schedule, budget) rather than continuous product ownership.

short_definition: A senior individual-contributor PM role, often leading a specific initiative or a small group of PMs without full people-management responsibility.
long_definition: Varies significantly in scope by company — at some organizations equivalent to Senior PM, at others a step toward Group PM.

short_definition: A PM who owns a platform — shared infrastructure, APIs, or services — used by other internal or external product teams, rather than a single customer-facing product.
long_definition: Requires thinking about internal 'customers' (other engineering/product teams) as much as or more than end users, and balancing broad reusability against any single team's specific needs.

short_definition: A designer responsible for a product's overall user experience, spanning research, interaction design, and visual design.
long_definition: See Product Design — the role title for the practitioner of that discipline.

short_definition: A role overseeing the process and execution of building products, often bridging product management and engineering management responsibilities.
long_definition: Title and scope vary significantly by company; sometimes closer to an engineering management role, sometimes closer to a senior PM role.

short_definition: A management-level role overseeing growth-focused product initiatives, often leading a team of growth PMs.
long_definition: See Growth Product Manager — the more senior/managerial version of the same specialization.

short_definition: A role (or PM responsibility) focused specifically on coordinating the cross-functional work needed to successfully launch a product or major feature.
long_definition: Common at larger companies where launches are complex enough to warrant a dedicated coordinator working across product, marketing, sales, and support.

short_definition: The discipline of guiding a product's development, strategy, and success by understanding customer needs, business goals, and market context.
long_definition: Sits at the intersection of business, technology, and user experience — often described (via a well-known Venn diagram) as the overlap of what's desirable, feasible, and viable.

short_definition: The pool of skilled product management professionals an organization can hire, develop, and retain.
long_definition: Referenced in discussions of PM hiring, career development programs, and building a strong product organization over time.

short_definition: The individual responsible for guiding a product's strategy, roadmap, and execution, working across engineering, design, and business stakeholders.
long_definition: Widely described as owning the 'what and why' of a product while engineering owns the 'how' — though the exact scope of the role varies significantly across companies and industries.

short_definition: A role responsible for positioning, messaging, and go-to-market strategy for a product — the bridge between product and the market.
long_definition: Distinct from a Product Manager: PMM owns how the product is communicated and sold, while PM owns what the product is and does. Close collaboration between the two is essential for a successful launch.

short_definition: A role (primarily in Scrum) responsible for maximizing product value by managing and prioritizing the product backlog.
long_definition: In many organizations the Product Owner and Product Manager roles are merged into one person; in others (especially larger, Scrum-heavy orgs) they're split, with the PO more focused on backlog/sprint-level execution and the PM on broader strategy.

short_definition: A role overseeing a portfolio of related products, balancing investment and strategy across the full set rather than managing a single product.
long_definition: See Product portfolio and Portfolio Management — the role responsible for that portfolio-level view.

short_definition: A role or specialization focused primarily on product strategy — market analysis, competitive positioning, and long-term direction — rather than day-to-day execution.
long_definition: Sometimes a distinct title, sometimes just describes the strategic aspect of a general PM's job, depending on the organization.

short_definition: The cross-functional group of people (PM, design, engineering, and often data/QA) responsible for a given product or product area.
long_definition: See Cross-Functional Team — 'product team' is the common name for this grouping as applied specifically to product development.

short_definition: The discipline of coordinating multiple related projects or workstreams toward a shared strategic objective.
long_definition: Broader in scope than managing a single project — a program manager typically coordinates across several teams or projects that individually contribute to a larger goal.

short_definition: A role responsible for Program Management — coordinating multiple related projects, dependencies, and stakeholders toward a shared goal.
long_definition: Distinct from a Product Manager (who owns product strategy/outcomes) and a Project Manager (who typically owns a single project's execution) — a Program Manager operates at a broader, cross-project coordination level.

short_definition: A role responsible for planning, executing, and delivering a specific project on time, within budget, and to scope.
long_definition: Focuses on execution and delivery mechanics (schedule, resources, risk) rather than product strategy — in some organizations this function is separate from the PM role, in others a PM covers both.

short_definition: A role in Scrum responsible for facilitating the process, removing team blockers, and coaching the team on Agile practices.
long_definition: Distinct from the Product Owner (who owns backlog priority/value) — the Scrum Master owns the team's process and ways of working, not the product content.

short_definition: Any individual or group with an interest in, or influence over, a product's success — including executives, customers, engineering, sales, and support.
long_definition: Managing stakeholder alignment and expectations is a core, ongoing part of the PM role, distinct from managing the product itself.

short_definition: A PM with deep technical fluency, often working on developer tools, APIs, or infrastructure products where engineering-level understanding is essential to making good roadmap calls.
long_definition: Distinguished from a general PM by the depth of technical knowledge required to credibly engage with engineering on architecture and technical tradeoffs, not just business requirements.

short_definition: A designer focused specifically on user experience — research, interaction design, and usability — as distinct from purely visual/UI design.
long_definition: See User Experience (UX) — the role title for a practitioner focused on that discipline, sometimes distinguished from a 'UI Designer' who focuses more narrowly on visual interface design.

short_definition: A set of rules that lets different software systems communicate with each other.
long_definition: See API (Application Programming Interface).

short_definition: A defined way for one piece of software to request data or functionality from another, without needing to know how the other system works internally.
long_definition: PMs need enough understanding of APIs to scope integration work, evaluate partner/platform opportunities, and have credible conversations with engineering about what's technically feasible to expose or consume.

short_definition: A program or piece of software designed to perform a specific set of functions for a user.
long_definition: General term encompassing web apps, mobile apps, and desktop software — used broadly rather than referring to any specific type.

short_definition: The process of verifying that a user is who they claim to be, typically via a password, token, or biometric.
long_definition: Often confused with Authorization — authentication answers 'who are you,' while authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do.'

short_definition: The process of determining what an authenticated user is allowed to access or do within a system.
long_definition: Comes after Authentication in the security flow — a user can be correctly authenticated (verified as who they are) but still be unauthorized for a given action or resource.

short_definition: The server-side part of an application — logic, databases, and infrastructure — that isn't directly visible to the user.
long_definition: Contrasted with Front-end (the client-facing UI); PMs need to know roughly what lives on which side to reason about where a given change or bug likely originates.

short_definition: An independent line of development in a version-control system, allowing changes to be made without affecting the main codebase until merged.
long_definition: Lets engineers work on features or fixes in isolation before integrating them — PMs encounter this concept when discussing release timing or when a feature is 'in a branch' vs. merged and shippable.

short_definition: An error or flaw in software that causes it to behave incorrectly or unexpectedly.
long_definition: Distinguished from a Defect in formal QA processes sometimes, but generally used interchangeably; tracked and triaged for severity/priority alongside feature work in the backlog.

short_definition: A temporary storage layer that keeps frequently accessed data readily available, so it doesn't need to be recomputed or refetched every time.
long_definition: Improves performance significantly but introduces its own class of bugs (stale/'cached' data) — PMs should recognize 'is this a caching issue' as a common engineering diagnosis for 'why isn't this updating.'

short_definition: A geographically distributed network of servers that caches and delivers content from a location close to the end user, improving load speed.
long_definition: Relevant to PMs when discussing performance and global scalability — a CDN reduces latency for users far from a company's primary servers.

short_definition: The practice of having other engineers examine code changes before they're merged, to catch bugs and maintain quality/consistency.
long_definition: A standard engineering quality practice; PMs benefit from knowing it's a normal part of the delivery timeline, not an optional extra step that can be skipped to hit a deadline.

short_definition: A lightweight, portable package that bundles an application with everything it needs to run consistently across different computing environments.
long_definition: Popularized by Docker; enables consistent deployment across development, testing, and production environments, and underpins much of modern cloud infrastructure (including Microservices architectures).

short_definition: Software designed to run on multiple operating systems or device types (e.g., iOS and Android) from largely the same codebase.
long_definition: A build strategy choice PMs weigh with engineering: cross-platform tools can speed up delivery across platforms but sometimes trade off native performance or platform-specific polish.

short_definition: An organized system for storing, managing, and retrieving data.
long_definition: PMs don't need to write database queries, but understanding basic database concepts (like why a schema change is a bigger deal than it sounds) helps in scoping technical work realistically.

short_definition: A flaw in software that causes it to not meet requirements or behave as intended — largely synonymous with Bug in most usage.
long_definition: See Bug.

short_definition: The client-facing part of an application — the interface and interactions a user directly sees and touches.
long_definition: Contrasted with Backend; front-end work covers everything from layout and styling to client-side logic that talks to backend APIs.

short_definition: A query language and API approach that lets clients request exactly the data they need in a single request, rather than multiple fixed endpoints.
long_definition: An alternative to traditional REST APIs; PMs may encounter GraphQL vs. REST as an architecture decision engineering makes, relevant mainly for its efficiency benefits with complex, nested data needs.

short_definition: A property of an operation where performing it multiple times produces the same result as performing it once.
long_definition: Important in system reliability — an idempotent API call (like 'set status to X') can be safely retried after a network failure without unintended side effects, unlike a non-idempotent one (like 'increment count by 1').

short_definition: The broad field encompassing computer systems, networks, and infrastructure used to store, process, and transmit data.
long_definition: General umbrella term; product organizations sit within or alongside a company's broader IT function, though product-focused software development and traditional IT operations are often organizationally distinct.

short_definition: A software application that provides developers with tools (code editor, debugger, build automation) in one integrated interface for writing software.
long_definition: Not typically PM-facing directly, but useful context for understanding the engineering workflow and tooling that supports development velocity.

short_definition: A test verifying that different components or systems work correctly together, as opposed to testing each in isolation.
long_definition: Sits between Unit Test (single component) and full end-to-end testing in the testing pyramid — catches issues that only appear when pieces interact.

short_definition: JavaScript Object Notation — a lightweight, human-readable data format widely used for exchanging data between systems, especially via APIs.
long_definition: The de facto standard format for API request/response data in modern web development; PMs will see it in API documentation and integration discussions.

short_definition: The delay between a user's action and the system's response.
long_definition: A key performance metric — high latency (a slow-feeling product) directly hurts user experience and can affect metrics like conversion and retention, even when functionality is otherwise correct.

short_definition: A system that distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent any single server from being overwhelmed.
long_definition: Key to reliability and Scalability — relevant when discussing how a product will handle traffic growth or spikes without downtime.

short_definition: An architecture style where an application is built as a collection of small, independently deployable services, rather than one large unified codebase.
long_definition: Contrasted with a Monolith; microservices can improve scalability and team autonomy but add operational complexity — a tradeoff PMs should understand when engineering weighs architecture decisions that affect delivery speed.

short_definition: A software architecture where the entire application is built and deployed as a single, unified codebase.
long_definition: Contrasted with Microservices; simpler to build and deploy initially, but can become harder to scale or modify independently as the codebase and team grow.

short_definition: An application built specifically for a particular platform (iOS or Android) using that platform's own tools and languages, as opposed to a cross-platform or web-based app.
long_definition: Generally offers the best performance and access to platform-specific features, at the cost of needing separate codebases per platform — a build strategy tradeoff PMs weigh with engineering.

short_definition: A category of databases that don't use the traditional relational (table-based, SQL) structure, often optimized for flexibility or scale with unstructured data.
long_definition: Contrasted with traditional relational (SQL) databases; the choice affects what kinds of data structures and queries are easy or hard to support, relevant when scoping data-heavy features.

short_definition: An open standard protocol that lets users grant a third-party application limited access to their account on another service, without sharing their password.
long_definition: The mechanism behind 'Sign in with Google/Facebook/etc.' and most third-party integrations — relevant whenever a PM scopes a feature involving connecting to an external account or service.

short_definition: A service that securely processes payment transactions between a customer, merchant, and financial institutions.
long_definition: PMs building any checkout or billing flow need to understand which payment gateway is being integrated and its constraints (supported payment methods, fees, compliance requirements like PCI-DSS).

short_definition: A collection of pre-written, reusable code that developers can call on to perform common functions without writing them from scratch.
long_definition: Using existing libraries speeds up development significantly compared to building every capability in-house — relevant context when engineering explains why a feature is faster or slower to build than expected.

short_definition: A web application built to behave like a native app — installable, capable of offline use, and able to send push notifications — while still running through a browser.
long_definition: An alternative to building separate native apps; can reduce development cost but historically has had some feature/performance limitations compared to true native apps, particularly on iOS.

short_definition: A request to merge a set of code changes from one branch into another, typically triggering a Code Review before the merge is approved.
long_definition: The standard mechanism engineers use to propose, review, and integrate changes; PMs may see PR status referenced as a proxy for how close a feature is to being merged and shippable.

short_definition: The discipline and process of testing software to identify defects and ensure it meets quality standards before release.
long_definition: Distinct from Unit Test/Integration Test (which are specific automated testing techniques) — QA broadly covers all testing activities, automated and manual, that happen before and around a release.

short_definition: A software bug that occurs when the behavior of a system depends on the unpredictable timing or ordering of concurrent operations.
long_definition: A notoriously tricky class of bug to reproduce and fix, since it may only occur under specific timing conditions — worth knowing as a category of issue that can take engineering longer to diagnose than a typical bug.

short_definition: A system that analyzes data (like past behavior) to suggest relevant content, products, or actions to a user.
long_definition: Powers features like 'you might also like' — PMs scoping personalization features need to understand what data and algorithmic approach the recommendation engine relies on.

short_definition: Restructuring existing code to improve its internal structure and maintainability, without changing its external behavior.
long_definition: Important 'invisible' engineering work that doesn't add new user-facing functionality but keeps the codebase healthy enough to build new features on top of quickly — PMs need to budget time for it, not just feature work.

short_definition: A bug where something that previously worked correctly stops working, usually as an unintended side effect of a new change.
long_definition: A key reason for regression testing (rerunning existing tests after a change) — a shipped feature breaking something unrelated is one of the most common and frustrating failure modes in software delivery.

short_definition: A storage location for a project's code and its version history, managed by a version-control system like Git.
long_definition: The basic unit of organization for a codebase — PMs will hear 'repo' used casually to refer to a specific project's codebase.

short_definition: A design/development approach that makes a web page or app adapt its layout to different screen sizes and devices.
long_definition: The standard practice for modern web products, given the wide range of device sizes users access a product from; see also Breakpoints.

short_definition: Representational State Transfer — an architectural style for designing networked APIs based on standard HTTP methods and resource-based URLs.
long_definition: The most common API design paradigm; see REST API for the applied concept.

short_definition: An API designed according to REST principles, using standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to interact with resources identified by URLs.
long_definition: The most widely used API architecture style; PMs encounter it when scoping integrations or partner API access.

short_definition: A system's ability to handle growing amounts of work (more users, more data, more traffic) without a significant drop in performance.
long_definition: A key non-functional requirement PMs need to consider early — a feature that works fine for 100 users may need real engineering investment to work for 1 million.

short_definition: A collection of tools, libraries, and documentation that helps developers build applications for a specific platform or integrate with a specific service.
long_definition: Relevant when a PM is scoping a platform strategy — offering an SDK is a common way to let third-party developers build on top of a product.

short_definition: The structured process a team follows to plan, build, test, and release software, typically including phases like requirements, design, development, testing, and deployment.
long_definition: A general umbrella term for the overall development process, regardless of whether the specific methodology used is Agile, Waterfall, or something else.

short_definition: The standard language used to query and manage data in relational databases.
long_definition: PMs don't need to write SQL to do their jobs, but basic familiarity helps when pulling simple data insights directly or understanding what analysts/engineers mean by 'running a query.'

short_definition: The combination of programming languages, frameworks, and tools used to build and run a product.
long_definition: PMs benefit from knowing their product's tech stack at a high level, since it affects hiring, third-party integration options, and what kinds of features are easy or hard to build.

short_definition: The amount of work (requests, transactions, data) a system can process in a given period of time.
long_definition: A key performance/capacity metric alongside Latency — relevant when discussing whether infrastructure can handle expected load.

short_definition: A security process requiring users to verify their identity through two different methods (e.g., password plus a code sent to their phone).
long_definition: A common security feature PMs are asked to scope for account protection — adds friction to login but significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized account access.

short_definition: An automated test that verifies a small, isolated piece of code (like a single function) behaves correctly.
long_definition: The smallest and fastest layer of the testing pyramid; a codebase with strong unit test coverage generally lets engineering ship changes with more confidence and speed.

short_definition: The practice of writing and running Unit Tests.
long_definition: See Unit Test.

short_definition: A system for tracking and managing changes to code (or other files) over time, allowing multiple people to collaborate without overwriting each other's work.
long_definition: Git is the dominant version control system in modern software development; foundational infrastructure that makes collaborative engineering work possible at scale.

short_definition: The practice of assigning identifiers (version numbers) to distinct states of a product, API, or codebase over time.
long_definition: Relevant to PMs when discussing API stability (breaking vs. non-breaking changes) or app release numbering communicated to users/partners.

short_definition: An automated message sent from one application to another when a specific event occurs, allowing real-time integration between systems.
long_definition: A common mechanism for integrations — e.g., 'notify our system whenever a payment succeeds' — relevant when scoping how a product connects to third-party tools.

short_definition: A communication protocol that allows a persistent, two-way connection between a client and server, enabling real-time data exchange.
long_definition: Used for features requiring live updates (chat, live notifications, collaborative editing) where constantly polling a server would be inefficient.

short_definition: Extensible Markup Language — a structured, tag-based data format, historically common for data exchange before JSON became more dominant.
long_definition: Still used in many legacy systems and specific industries (e.g., certain enterprise or government integrations); PMs may encounter it when integrating with older systems.

short_definition: The practice of preparing, supporting, and helping people adopt a change (process, tool, or product) successfully.
long_definition: Overlaps with Change Management but leans more toward practical enablement — training, documentation, and support that helps a change actually stick.

short_definition: A structured approach to preparing an organization or its customers for a significant change, minimizing disruption and resistance.
long_definition: Relevant when a product update significantly changes an existing workflow — good change management (communication, training, phased rollout) reduces user backlash and support burden.

short_definition: The underlying guidelines and best practices that inform effective Change Management efforts.
long_definition: See Change Management.

short_definition: An internal review gate where a proposed product concept is evaluated by stakeholders before it proceeds to fuller investment.
long_definition: An early checkpoint in a product development process meant to catch weak ideas before significant resources are committed.

short_definition: The process of moving data from one system, format, or storage location to another.
long_definition: A common source of technical risk in product changes (platform migrations, replatforming) — PMs scoping this kind of work need to account for data integrity checks and potential downtime.

short_definition: A discipline focused on optimizing the design team's processes, tools, and workflows so designers can focus on design work rather than operational overhead.
long_definition: The design-team counterpart to Product Operations — manages things like design tooling, design system governance, and cross-team design processes.

short_definition: The process of designing and planning how an organization's technology systems, data, and processes should be structured to support business strategy.
long_definition: Typically a broader, company-wide activity than a single product roadmap; product teams may need to align their plans with enterprise architecture constraints in larger organizations.

short_definition: A plan showing how an organization's enterprise architecture will evolve over time.
long_definition: See Enterprise Architecture Planning — the roadmap artifact that communicates the planned evolution.

short_definition: Systems and processes for collecting, organizing, and acting on feedback at scale across a large organization's many products or customer touchpoints.
long_definition: Relevant for large enterprises with feedback coming from many products, regions, or channels that need centralized management rather than ad hoc handling.

short_definition: A distinct instance of a software system's infrastructure used for a specific purpose (e.g., development, testing, staging, production).
long_definition: PMs will hear features described as being 'in staging' or 'in prod' — understanding environments helps clarify exactly what stage a feature is at before it's live for real users.

short_definition: A systematic review of a product's existing features to assess their usage, value, and whether they should be kept, improved, or removed.
long_definition: Helps prevent feature bloat by periodically checking whether every feature still earns its place in the product.

short_definition: The accumulation of too many features in a product, making it complex, cluttered, or harder to use.
long_definition: A common failure mode when teams keep adding features without regularly pruning underused or low-value ones — see Feature Audit as a corrective practice.

short_definition: The gradual, often unplanned expansion of a specific feature's scope beyond its original intent.
long_definition: Similar to Scope creep but specifically at the feature level — a feature that keeps growing in complexity as more edge cases and requests get added.

short_definition: A critical term for a product organization that ships features continuously without connecting them to measurable outcomes or user value.
long_definition: A cautionary label — 'feature factory' teams optimize for output (number of things shipped) rather than outcome (whether those things actually help users or the business).

short_definition: A meeting or process step marking the formal start of work on a specific feature, aligning the team on scope and goals before development begins.
long_definition: Ensures everyone involved (design, engineering, QA) starts with a shared understanding rather than discovering misalignment mid-build.

short_definition: A review conducted after a feature ships to evaluate whether it achieved its intended goals.
long_definition: Closes the loop between the goal a feature was built to achieve and the actual result — without this step, teams risk continuing to invest in features that aren't working.

short_definition: The act of making a new feature available to users.
long_definition: Can range from a full public launch to a controlled Feature Flag rollout to a subset of users, depending on the release strategy.

short_definition: A numeric value assigned to a feature idea based on a prioritization framework, used to rank it against other candidates.
long_definition: The output of applying frameworks like RICE or ICE to a specific feature — used to compare and sequence backlog items.

short_definition: Plural of Feature — the discrete pieces of functionality that make up a product.
long_definition: See Feature Audit, Feature Bloat, and related entries for how features are managed as a portfolio, not just individually.

short_definition: A cycle where the output or results of an action inform and adjust future action — in product terms, using user feedback/data to continuously improve the product.
long_definition: A core concept behind iterative product development; a short, tight feedback loop lets teams learn and adjust faster than a slow, infrequent one.

short_definition: The systematic process of collecting, organizing, prioritizing, and acting on feedback from users or stakeholders.
long_definition: See Customer Feedback Analysis and Enterprise Feedback Management for related, more specific practices.

short_definition: A running list of product ideas that haven't yet been vetted, prioritized, or committed to the main backlog.
long_definition: Serves as an intake point for ideas from any source (customers, team members, leadership) before they're evaluated and potentially promoted into the actual product backlog.

short_definition: The process of capturing, evaluating, and tracking ideas from intake through to a decision about whether to pursue them.
long_definition: Distinct from Innovation Management in scope — idea management is often the more tactical, day-to-day intake and triage process feeding into broader innovation strategy.

short_definition: The process an organization follows to detect, respond to, and resolve unplanned service disruptions or outages.
long_definition: PMs are often involved in incident response for customer communication and post-incident review, even if they don't own the technical resolution itself.

short_definition: An older product (or version) that's still in use but based on outdated technology, architecture, or design compared to current standards.
long_definition: Legacy products often require ongoing maintenance investment and create tension with newer product priorities — a common source of roadmap tradeoff discussions.

short_definition: A detailed, step-by-step document outlining exactly how to execute a specific operational task, often used for high-risk changes like deployments or migrations.
long_definition: Common in operations-heavy or infrastructure contexts, ensuring a risky procedure is executed consistently and with a clear rollback plan if something goes wrong.

short_definition: The practice of overseeing and balancing investment across a company's full set of products or initiatives.
long_definition: Operates at a level above individual product roadmaps — decides how much investment goes to which products, and when to sunset underperforming ones.

short_definition: A cross-functional governance group (often senior leaders) that reviews and approves major product decisions, investments, or direction changes.
long_definition: Provides a formal decision-making body for significant product bets, especially in larger organizations where individual PMs don't have unilateral authority over big investments.

short_definition: The process of building and shipping product work, as distinct from the discovery/strategy work that decides what to build.
long_definition: The 'delivery' side of the discovery/delivery split discussed under Dual-Track Agile — focused on execution once direction is set.

short_definition: The recurring sequence of stages (idea, design, build, test, launch) a product or feature moves through from concept to release.
long_definition: See Product Development Process — largely interchangeable terms describing the same overall flow.

short_definition: The defined sequence of steps and gates an organization follows to move a product idea from concept to launch.
long_definition: Varies significantly by company — some use lightweight, continuous flows (Agile/Lean), others use more formal stage-gate processes with defined checkpoints.

short_definition: Providing internal teams (sales, support, marketing) with the knowledge, materials, and training needed to sell, support, or represent a product effectively.
long_definition: Product Marketing often leads this, but PMs are usually the source of the underlying product knowledge that gets translated into enablement materials.

short_definition: The set of functional capabilities that make up a product, viewed collectively.
long_definition: See Features.

short_definition: The stages a product goes through from introduction through growth, maturity, and eventual decline or sunset.
long_definition: A classic strategic framework for thinking about how a product's priorities and investment level should shift as it matures — a growth-stage product needs different things than a mature, stable one.

short_definition: A structured review of a product management team's practices, processes, and output to assess maturity or identify improvement areas.
long_definition: Often conducted by leadership or an external consultant to benchmark a PM organization's effectiveness.

short_definition: Software used specifically to support product management work — roadmapping, backlog management, feedback collection, and analytics.
long_definition: Examples of the category include tools like Productboard and Aha! — PMs' day-to-day toolkit for managing the artifacts and processes covered elsewhere in this glossary.

short_definition: The category of software tools PMs use to do their jobs, spanning roadmapping, analytics, feedback, and collaboration tools.
long_definition: See Product Management Platform — broader term for the same category of supporting software.

short_definition: The process of introducing a new user to a product, distinct from employee onboarding.
long_definition: See Onboarding — this entry specifically disambiguates the product-usage meaning from the (also common) HR meaning of the word.

short_definition: A discipline that provides the tools, processes, and data infrastructure product teams need to work efficiently, similar to how Sales Ops or DesignOps support their functions.
long_definition: Handles things like roadmap tooling, feedback systems, and process standardization across product teams, freeing individual PMs to focus on strategy and execution rather than operational overhead.

short_definition: The ongoing practice of refining a product's features and experience to improve performance against key goals.
long_definition: General umbrella term for continuous improvement work — could involve UX tweaks, performance improvements, or feature refinements based on data and feedback.

short_definition: The process of deciding what a product team will work on and in what sequence, translating strategy into an actionable roadmap.
long_definition: Sits between Product Strategy (the why) and execution (the how) — the activity of turning strategic priorities into a concrete, sequenced plan.

short_definition: The discipline of managing a company's full set of products as a coordinated portfolio, balancing investment, risk, and strategic fit.
long_definition: See Portfolio Management — this entry applies the concept specifically to a company's product line.

short_definition: The ongoing process of capturing, organizing, and maintaining a product's requirements throughout its development lifecycle.
long_definition: Encompasses more than writing a single PRD — includes managing requirement changes, traceability, and version history as a product evolves.

short_definition: A high-level, visual plan showing the direction a product will take over time — the themes, priorities, and (sometimes) rough timing of upcoming work.
long_definition: Communicates strategic intent to stakeholders without necessarily committing to exact dates or a fixed feature list; formats vary from timeline-based to outcome/theme-based depending on the organization's philosophy about how much certainty to project.

short_definition: A plan showing the timeline and milestones for a specific project, as distinct from an ongoing product's broader roadmap.
long_definition: More time-bound and execution-focused than a Product Roadmap, which spans a product's ongoing evolution rather than a single bounded project.

short_definition: Removing or correcting a product (or, in a data-quality sense, a metric) that was found to be defective or problematic after release.
long_definition: In a product-safety or quality sense, distinct from the machine-learning statistical metric of the same name — context determines which meaning applies.

short_definition: The process of planning, scheduling, and controlling how and when software releases move through development to production.
long_definition: Coordinates the many moving pieces (code readiness, QA, stakeholder communication, rollback plans) involved in getting a release out safely and predictably.

short_definition: Software specifically designed to help teams build, visualize, and communicate product roadmaps.
long_definition: See Product Management Platform — roadmapping tools are one common category within the broader PM software landscape.

short_definition: Technology systems or tools used within an organization without explicit approval or oversight from the central IT department.
long_definition: Relevant to PMs building enterprise/internal tools — shadow IT often emerges when official tools don't meet a team's needs, and can be a signal of unmet product requirements.

short_definition: A pre-production environment that closely mirrors the live production system, used for final testing before a release goes live.
long_definition: The last checkpoint before production — catches issues that only show up in a production-like setting, which a local development environment might not reveal.

short_definition: The practice of identifying stakeholders and understanding their interests, influence, and expectations regarding a product or initiative.
long_definition: Helps PMs plan communication and manage competing priorities by understanding who cares about what, and how much influence they have over the outcome.

short_definition: The ongoing practice of communicating with, aligning, and managing the expectations of the various stakeholders involved in or affected by a product.
long_definition: A significant, continuous part of the PM role — as much about relationship management and clear communication as it is about the product itself.

short_definition: Internal testing of a product or feature, conducted by employees or a very limited group, before wider external testing.
long_definition: The earliest, most limited testing stage — meant to catch major issues before the product is exposed to any real (external) users.

short_definition: The activity/phase of conducting Alpha Test testing.
long_definition: See Alpha Test.

short_definition: Testing a product or feature with a limited group of real external users before general release.
long_definition: Comes after Alpha Test in the typical release progression — provides real-world feedback and surfaces issues internal testing might miss, while still limiting exposure/risk.

short_definition: See Beta Test — testing with a limited group of real external users before general release.
long_definition: See Beta Test.

short_definition: A software engineering practice of automatically integrating, testing, and preparing code changes for release frequently and reliably.
long_definition: CI (Continuous Integration) means frequently merging code changes with automated testing; CD can mean Continuous Delivery (code is always in a releasable state, but deployment is a manual trigger) or Continuous Deployment (every passing change deploys automatically) — worth being clear on which CD is meant.
