short_definition: A practice where code changes are automatically prepared for a release to production, but the actual release is triggered manually.
long_definition: Sits between Continuous Integration and full Continuous Deployment — every change is release-ready, but a human decides when to actually ship it.

short_definition: A practice where every code change that passes automated tests is automatically released to production, with no manual approval step.
long_definition: The most automated end of the CI/CD spectrum — requires high confidence in automated testing, since there's no human gate before changes reach real users.

short_definition: A practice where developers frequently merge their code changes into a shared codebase, with automated builds and tests run on each merge.
long_definition: Catches integration issues early and often, rather than letting them accumulate until a large, risky merge — the 'CI' in CI/CD.

short_definition: The process of releasing a new version of software to a live environment where it becomes available for use.
long_definition: Can refer to deploying to any environment (staging, production) but most often means releasing to production, making a change live for real users.

short_definition: A set of practices and culture combining software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) to enable faster, more reliable software delivery.
long_definition: Emphasizes automation, collaboration between traditionally separate teams, and continuous delivery — the organizational/cultural counterpart to technical practices like CI/CD.

short_definition: The point at which a product, feature, or version is officially discontinued and no longer supported or maintained.
long_definition: A planned event PMs manage deliberately, including customer communication and migration paths, rather than something that just happens passively.

short_definition: A configuration switch that lets teams turn a feature on or off (or roll it out to a subset of users) without deploying new code.
long_definition: A powerful tool for controlled, gradual rollouts and quick rollback if something goes wrong — lets teams decouple deploying code from actually releasing a feature to users.

short_definition: The stage at which a product or feature is fully released and available to all customers, with full support commitments.
long_definition: The final stage after earlier phases like Alpha, Beta, or limited rollout — signals the feature is considered stable and production-ready for everyone.

short_definition: A document communicating what changed in a new release — new features, fixes, and known issues.
long_definition: Serves both external users (what's new) and internal teams (support, sales) who need to know what changed to do their jobs.

short_definition: A plan outlining what will be included in an upcoming release and the timeline/process for getting it out.
long_definition: Coordinates the scope, sequencing, and readiness checks (QA, documentation, communication) needed before a release ships.

short_definition: Reverting a system to a previous version after a deployment causes problems.
long_definition: A critical safety mechanism — the ability to quickly and reliably roll back is why teams invest in good deployment practices and Feature Flags, which make rollback faster than a full redeploy.

short_definition: Common shorthand in tech for releasing a product or feature to users.
long_definition: Casual, ubiquitous term ('we shipped it Friday') — used interchangeably with 'release' or 'launch,' though 'ship' often implies a smaller/incremental release rather than a major launch event.

short_definition: The deliberate process of winding down and eventually discontinuing a product or feature.
long_definition: See End-of-Life (EOL) — sunsetting emphasizes the gradual, managed process (communication, migration support) rather than just the final discontinuation date.

short_definition: The implied future cost of choosing a faster, easier engineering solution now instead of a better, more robust one — the accumulated cost of shortcuts.
long_definition: Like financial debt, it can be a reasonable tradeoff in the short term but accrues 'interest' (slower future development, more bugs) if never paid down — PMs need to budget time to address it, not just keep adding features on top.

short_definition: Testing performed by actual end users (or their representatives) to confirm a product meets their needs before final release.
long_definition: The final validation step before release, focused on real-world usability and correctness from the user's perspective rather than just technical functionality.

short_definition: A pricing strategy where a core product is sold cheaply (or at a loss) while complementary, required add-ons are sold at a higher margin.
long_definition: Classic example: cheap printers with expensive ink cartridges. Relevant to PMs designing pricing/packaging strategy for products with a core-plus-consumables or core-plus-add-ons structure.

short_definition: The process of bringing a product to market and turning it into a revenue-generating business offering.
long_definition: Encompasses pricing, packaging, sales enablement, and launch — the business-facing counterpart to the technical work of building the product.

short_definition: A systematic evaluation of competitors' products, strategies, and positioning to inform a company's own strategy.
long_definition: A foundational input to Product Strategy and Positioning — helps a team understand where they have a genuine advantage versus where they're just following the market.

short_definition: The ongoing practice of gathering and analyzing information about competitors to inform strategic decisions.
long_definition: Distinct from a one-time Competitive Analysis — competitive intelligence is a continuous monitoring function, often owned by product marketing or a dedicated team in larger organizations.

short_definition: The overall set of competitors and alternative solutions a product competes against in its market.
long_definition: Understanding the full landscape (including indirect competitors and substitute solutions, not just direct competitors) is essential for accurate Positioning.

short_definition: Same as Competitive Analysis — evaluating competitors to inform strategy.
long_definition: See Competitive Analysis.

short_definition: A system and set of practices for managing a company's interactions and relationships with current and prospective customers, typically centered on a CRM software platform.
long_definition: PMs building sales or customer-facing tools frequently need to integrate with a CRM (like Salesforce or HubSpot), since it's often the system of record for customer/account data.

short_definition: Making a product or feature available to a limited group of users before its full public release.
long_definition: Similar to Beta Test but often framed more as a marketing/exclusivity opportunity than a pure testing exercise — used to build anticipation and gather early feedback simultaneously.

short_definition: A customer segment willing to try new products before they're widely proven, often more tolerant of rough edges in exchange for being first.
long_definition: A key audience for early product validation and Beta Test programs; per Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovation model, early adopters come right after 'innovators' and ahead of the mainstream majority.

short_definition: The plan for how a product will reach its target customers and achieve adoption — covering positioning, pricing, channels, and launch approach.
long_definition: Coordinates product, marketing, and sales around a shared plan for how a specific product or feature will actually get in front of, and adopted by, its intended customers.

short_definition: Communications (announcements, tips, prompts) delivered to users directly within a product's interface, rather than via email or other external channels.
long_definition: A common channel for onboarding guidance, feature announcements, and engagement nudges, since it reaches users at the moment they're already using the product.

short_definition: Designing and building a product so it can be adapted to different languages, regions, and cultures without requiring engineering rework for each one.
long_definition: The technical groundwork (often abbreviated i18n) that makes Localization possible — internationalization is the enabling architecture; localization is the actual per-market adaptation.

short_definition: The specific areas of responsibility or outcome a role or team is accountable for, used to define performance expectations.
long_definition: A broader, more qualitative performance-management concept than the more specific, measurable Key Results within an OKR framework, though the terms are sometimes used loosely and interchangeably.

short_definition: Software used to deliver, track, and manage training or educational content.
long_definition: Relevant to PMs building products with an internal or customer-facing training/certification component, or when a company evaluates LMS platforms for internal enablement.

short_definition: Adapting a product's content, language, currency, and cultural references for a specific market or region.
long_definition: Builds on Internationalization's technical foundation — localization is the market-specific execution, translating and adjusting content for a given locale.

short_definition: Research into a market's size, trends, customer needs, and competitive dynamics to inform strategic decisions.
long_definition: A foundational input to product strategy and go-to-market planning, typically conducted before or alongside a significant product investment decision.

short_definition: Dividing a broad market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics.
long_definition: Enables more targeted product, pricing, and messaging decisions than treating the whole market as homogeneous; see also User Segment for the product-usage-focused counterpart.

short_definition: Confirming, through real evidence, that there is genuine market demand for a product idea before fully committing resources to build it.
long_definition: A go-to-market-oriented complement to Customer Validation — focuses on whether a broad enough market exists, not just whether individual customers respond well.

short_definition: A critical point in the customer experience that significantly shapes their perception of a brand or product, positive or negative.
long_definition: A marketing/CX concept (popularized by Procter & Gamble) highlighting that certain interactions — first use, a support issue, a renewal decision — matter disproportionately to overall customer sentiment.

short_definition: A strategy providing a seamless, integrated customer experience across multiple channels (web, mobile, in-store, support) that work together rather than in isolation.
long_definition: Distinct from simply being present on multiple channels — omnichannel specifically means those channels are connected and consistent, so a customer's experience carries over between them.

short_definition: The overall approach a company takes to setting prices for its products, balancing customer willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and business goals.
long_definition: A major strategic lever PMs influence — pricing model choice (subscription, usage-based, freemium, tiered) shapes growth dynamics as much as the product itself does.

short_definition: The coordinated release of a new product or major feature to the market, typically involving marketing, sales, and support alongside the product team.
long_definition: Distinguished from a routine Feature Release by its scale and cross-functional coordination — a launch is a planned event, not just a deploy.

short_definition: The discipline of planning and coordinating all the cross-functional work required for a successful product launch.
long_definition: See Product Launch Manager — the practice that role is responsible for executing.

short_definition: The schedule of milestones and activities leading up to and following a product launch.
long_definition: Coordinates dependencies across product, marketing, sales, and support so all pieces (documentation, training, press, in-product rollout) are ready by launch day.

short_definition: The discipline responsible for positioning, messaging, and go-to-market execution for a product.
long_definition: See Product Marketing Manager — the function that role owns, bridging product and the market.

short_definition: A measure of how much profit a product generates relative to the cost of building and operating it.
long_definition: A key input to portfolio decisions — informs which products deserve continued investment and which may need to be sunset or restructured.

short_definition: A go-to-market strategy where the product itself — not sales or marketing — is the primary driver of customer acquisition, conversion, and expansion.
long_definition: Relies on users being able to discover, try, and get value from a product with minimal friction (often via free trials or freemium tiers) before ever talking to sales — a major shift from traditional sales-led B2B go-to-market.

short_definition: The organizational function focused on researching and developing new products, technologies, or significant improvements to existing ones.
long_definition: Broader than a single product team's discovery work — R&D often refers to a company-wide or division-wide function, sometimes encompassing more exploratory, longer-horizon work than typical product roadmaps.

short_definition: The stages a prospective customer moves through from initial awareness to becoming a paying customer.
long_definition: The sales-specific version of the general Funnel concept — tracked to identify where prospects are dropping off in the buying process.

short_definition: The set of active deals or prospects a sales team is currently working, organized by stage.
long_definition: Distinct from the Sales Funnel (a conceptual model of stages) — the pipeline is the actual, current inventory of real opportunities moving through those stages.

short_definition: The general practice of dividing a broader group (market, users, customers) into distinct subgroups based on shared characteristics.
long_definition: See Market Segmentation and User Segment for the specific applications of this general concept.

short_definition: The portion of the Total Addressable Market that a company's specific product or service could realistically serve, given its business model and geography.
long_definition: Narrower than TAM — accounts for practical constraints like current product capabilities, target geography, or channel reach.

short_definition: The portion of the Serviceable Addressable Market a company can realistically capture given competition, resources, and go-to-market execution.
long_definition: The narrowest of the TAM/SAM/SOM trio — represents a more realistic near-term revenue opportunity than the larger, more theoretical TAM figure.

short_definition: The total revenue opportunity available for a product or service if it captured 100% of the possible market.
long_definition: The broadest of the TAM/SAM/SOM framework — useful for understanding the ceiling of an opportunity, though rarely achievable in practice; see SAM and SOM for the narrower, more realistic figures.

short_definition: The specific group of customers a product is designed and marketed to serve.
long_definition: A foundational strategic decision — a well-defined target market focuses product and marketing decisions, rather than trying to appeal to everyone.

short_definition: The process of selecting and focusing on specific customer segments to pursue with marketing or product efforts.
long_definition: The action taken after Market Segmentation identifies distinct groups — deciding which of those segments to actually prioritize.

short_definition: A distinct level of a product's pricing or feature offering (e.g., Free, Pro, Enterprise), each with different features and price points.
long_definition: Central to Pricing Strategy for products using tiered pricing models — PMs decide what capabilities differentiate each tier to encourage upgrades.

short_definition: Any point of interaction between a customer and a company, across the product, marketing, sales, or support.
long_definition: The individual points mapped out in a Customer Journey — understanding each touchpoint's role helps identify where the experience succeeds or breaks down.

short_definition: An approach that integrates all sales channels, inventory, and customer data into a single, connected system rather than separate siloed channels.
long_definition: An evolution beyond Omnichannel, emphasizing a single backend system unifying the customer and operational data across all channels, not just a consistent front-end experience.

short_definition: A clear statement of what makes a product distinctly better or different from competitors, used to guide marketing and sales messaging.
long_definition: Closely related to Value Proposition and Positioning — the USP is often the most concise, sales-facing distillation of why a customer should choose this product.

short_definition: The specific factor that makes a product different from and better than competing alternatives, from a marketing/sales perspective.
long_definition: See Unique Selling Proposition — same concept, alternate phrasing.

short_definition: The systematic collection and representation of customer needs, expectations, and preferences, gathered directly from customers.
long_definition: An umbrella term for aggregating input across many feedback channels (surveys, interviews, support tickets) into a coherent view of what customers actually want.

canonical_term: What Is a Product Operating Model?
short_definition: A framework describing how a company organizes its people, processes, and structure to build and manage products effectively.
long_definition: Popularized in discussions (e.g., Marty Cagan's work) contrasting a strong 'product operating model' — empowered, outcome-focused product teams — against feature-factory or project-based ways of organizing product work.
